901: B is correct because migrating to a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for SQL Server DB instance is a managed service that significantly reduces operational overhead compared to running SQL Server on EC2, while the Multi-AZ deployment provides high availability with automatic failover to a standby in another Availability Zone. Using an AWS KMS managed key for encryption at rest increases security for the sensitive data. EC2 still requires the company to manage the OS, patching, and database administration, and S3 or DynamoDB cannot host relational SQL Server databases.
902: A is correct because an Auto Scaling group spanning two Availability Zones with an Application Load Balancer provides high availability, self-healing, and automatic scaling to increase the application's availability. AWS WAF integrates directly with an ALB, so attaching the WAF to the ALB protects the application from web exploits. A WAF cannot be attached to a placement group or an Auto Scaling group, and two static EC2 instances offer no automatic scaling or recovery.
903: A is correct because S3 access points provide a dedicated, application-specific entry point into a shared bucket, and each access point policy can restrict that application to only its specific prefix with granular object-level permissions. This is managed natively by S3 with the least operational overhead. ACLs per object, replication to separate buckets, and replication combined with access points all add significant cost and administration without the same simplicity.
904: A is correct because S3 Event Notifications can capture each image upload in near real time, and an SQS queue decouples the upload from processing while buffering messages durably. AWS Lambda is ideal for a 2-minute, 512 MB processing job and is far more cost-effective than continuously running compute, since it only runs and charges when messages arrive. Reserved Instances, always-on containers, and Elastic Beanstalk environments would run and cost money around the clock for sporadic, short workloads.
905: A is correct because AWS Global Accelerator uses static anycast IP addresses and the AWS global network to route traffic to healthy load balancer endpoints across Regions, improving both availability and performance for the stateful TCP-based and UDP-based components. D is correct because the Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and supports both TCP and UDP traffic, so an NLB in each Region can handle the stateful TCP workload on the EC2 endpoints and the stateless UDP workload routed to the on-premises endpoints. Application Load Balancers only support HTTP and HTTPS, which cannot handle the UDP traffic in this architecture.
906: C is correct because EBS snapshot retention rules in the Recycle Bin protect snapshots from accidental or malicious deletion by holding them in a recoverable state for a specified number of days after deletion. A 7-day rule ensures snapshots can be recovered after the cleaning script runs, without retaining them indefinitely, and it requires only a configuration change with the least development effort. Cross-Region copies and S3 copies add cost and complexity, and denying deletion would prevent the legitimate expiration cleanup.
907: C is correct because a presigned URL grants time-limited, secure access to the template object in the private S3 bucket without changing the bucket's public access block settings. This follows the security best practice of keeping the object private and providing scoped, temporary access only when a user requests the environment. Allowing public access or routing through API Gateway or a VPC endpoint adds unnecessary exposure or configuration complexity.
908: A is correct because IAM Identity Center provides centralized, federated console access for external users without creating long-lived local IAM users, and Systems Manager Session Manager with the SSM Agent and an instance profile enables OS access to private EC2 instances over an IAM-authorized, audited channel. This eliminates the need for SSH key pairs, bastion hosts, and open inbound ports on the instances. The other options rely on less secure patterns such as shared local IAM credentials, SSH exposure, or public bastion hosts.
909: D is correct because a read replica in the same Region (us-east-1) offloads the near-real-time ML report workload from the primary database, improving performance during business hours, and it avoids the higher cost and replication lag of a cross-Region replica. It is the most cost-effective option since it stays within one Region while still providing read scaling. Multi-AZ standby instances cannot serve read traffic, and using DMS to replicate to a new database adds cost and operational effort.
910: B is correct because enabling detailed monitoring on EC2 instances changes CloudWatch metric granularity from 5 minutes to 1-minute intervals, which satisfies the requirement to analyze performance with a granularity of no more than 2 minutes. CloudWatch metrics can then be used directly for near-real-time analysis without building a data pipeline. The log-based options involving Redshift and QuickSight add complexity and are not needed for 1-minute metric data.
911: C is correct because an S3 event notification triggers an AWS Lambda function each time a new photo is uploaded, allowing the thumbnail to be generated and stored immediately with a fully serverless, pay-per-use model. With only about 150 photos per day, Lambda is far more cost-effective than an always-on EC2 instance or a long-running EMR cluster that would run continuously. S3 Storage Lens is a metrics and reporting feature and cannot invoke Lambda functions.
912: D is correct because S3 Inventory generates reports of all objects, and an AWS Lambda function can filter that inventory to identify objects older than 3 years while excluding the data that must be retained. S3 Batch Operations then invokes the Lambda function at scale to delete the matching objects, providing a fully serverless solution that handles millions of objects. Options involving scripts on EC2, AWS Batch, or Glue crawlers require provisioning or custom orchestration and are not serverless.
913: C is correct because creating individual IAM roles for each Lambda function, granting each role only the specific S3 access it needs, and assigning each as its Lambda execution role enforces the principle of least privilege. This ensures only the authorized functions can retrieve the sensitive data, with permissions scoped per function. A shared role with full bucket access is over-privileged, and bucket policies cannot grant access based on Lambda function ARNs or rely on VPC endpoint IPs reliably, since Lambda does not have a concept of granting access by function ARN in this way.
914: B is correct because Amazon CloudFront with an S3-hosted static frontend provides global availability and low latency, while Lambda functions accessed through Amazon API Gateway offer a serverless, secure backend that eliminates server management. Migrating the MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL provides a managed database with automated patching, backups, and Multi-AZ availability, minimizing operational overhead. Reserved EC2 instances for the database still require self-management, and Lambda functions in a target group behind a load balancer is not a standard pattern for this architecture.
915: C is correct because Amazon ElastiCache for Redis provides fast in-memory access for near real-time reviews and rankings, and Redis supports data persistence through RDB snapshots and AOF logging, so the player data survives an application restart. This is a fully managed service with the least operational overhead. Memcached is purely in-memory with no persistence, and S3 or self-managed EC2 instances either lack real-time performance or add heavy management burden.
916: D is correct because creating separate KMS keys for each customer's data ensures each customer's data is encrypted independently, while granular key policies and CloudTrail logging provide the required access control and auditability for compliance. AWS KMS is a secure, centralized, fully managed key management service, so this meets the requirement with the least operational overhead. Storing keys in S3, deploying hardware appliances, or using a single key for all customers either lacks security or fails the per-customer separation requirement.
917: D is correct because an Application Load Balancer distributes incoming web traffic, and EC2 Auto Scaling groups automatically add capacity to handle traffic increases without degrading the customer experience. Amazon SQS durably stores unprocessed orders so no customer orders are lost during spikes or failures, and Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ provides highly available, durable storage for processed orders. The other options misuse technologies like NAT gateways, Gateway Load Balancers, or Redshift in ways that do not provide this resilient, decoupled order-processing flow.
918: A is correct because grouping millions of 10 KB files into large objects with an archive tool avoids the high per-object overhead and slow transfer of many small files, and DataSync can migrate those grouped objects efficiently. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides immediate (millisecond) access at a low storage cost, meeting the requirement that files be immediately available during the first year, and a lifecycle configuration transitions them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for the lowest-cost 7-year archival. Storing in Standard-IA or Flexible Retrieval either costs more for the access pattern or fails the immediate retrieval requirement.
919: A is correct because io1 volumes are capped at 64,000 provisioned IOPS per volume, so the single existing volume cannot deliver more IOPS on its own. Adding multiple io1 volumes and striping them with LVM aggregates their IOPS to exceed the 64,000 limit and improves throughput to match the on-premises performance. Increasing the volume size or IOPS on a single volume cannot exceed the per-volume cap, and changing only the instance type does not address the EBS volume's IOPS ceiling.
920: D is correct because an API Gateway HTTP API is significantly cheaper than a REST API while still invoking the Lambda publisher, and publishing events to an SNS topic with multiple subscribers implements the pub/sub pattern with event-driven, loosely coupled microservices. HTTP APIs provide the core request routing at lower cost, making this the most cost-effective option. REST and WebSocket APIs or Kinesis Data Streams cost more than needed for this simple publish/subscribe event flow.
